title: Assessing Priority Program Evaluation Training Needs of University of Kentucky Extension Agents: Implications for Building Evaluation Capacity
text_snippet: Assessing Priority Program Evaluation Training Needs of University of Kentucky Extension Agents: Implications for Building Evaluation Capacity Extension professionals play a crucial role in translating research into actionable knowledge, through evidence-based programming, to improve the livelihoods of individuals and communities. However, previous research has identified gaps in Extension agents’ evaluation skills, hence the need for evaluation capacity building efforts to enhance their evaluation competencies. This study presents the findings of a cross-sectional assessment aimed at identifying priority evaluation training needs of county-based Extension agents and whether these priority needs differ by agents’ education level, program area, and years of service in Extension. Data was collected from 341 University of Kentucky Extension agents who rated the extent to which they needed education on 21 evaluation topics. Results revealed eight top-priority evaluation topics including determining the economic value of programs, developing measurable medium- and long-term evaluation outcomes, conducting follow-up surveys, collecting real-time data from participants, developing effective quantitative data collection tools, utilizing online survey tools, and adapting existing questionnaires. title: Into the Metaverse: Exploring How Teacher Professional Development Influences Intent to Use Virtual Reality in the Classroom
text_snippet: Into the Metaverse: Exploring How Teacher Professional Development Influences Intent to Use Virtual Reality in the Classroom This study utilized Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explore how school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers' participation in the Agriscience Metaverse Academy (AMA) influenced their intent to integrate virtual reality (VR) into curriculum. The AMA program included a five-day workshop that provided 28 teachers in Tennessee and Nebraska with VR headsets, training, and opportunities to create VR-enhanced lessons. We used qualitative methods to fulfill the purpose of this study, and focus groups were conducted with participants following workshop completion. A priori coding for the TPB variables was used to analyze the focus group transcripts, and the data revealed that participants generally held positive attitudes about VR's potential to increase student engagement. However, they also harbored concerns regarding classroom and technology management. Although subjective norms were sometimes mentioned positively, participants often anticipated skepticism about VR technology from their peers and administrators. title: Agriculture and Science Teachers’ Agricultural Misconceptions Before and After an Intensive 10-Day Agricultural Science Professional Development Institute
text_snippet: Agriculture and Science Teachers’ Agricultural Misconceptions Before and After an Intensive 10-Day Agricultural Science Professional Development Institute Because understanding of scientific concepts in rural communities may improve when concepts are linked to agriculture, we developed an intensive agricultural science professional development (PD) program for grades 5-12 teachers in the southeastern USA that included content and demonstrations presented by agricultural science experts, immersive field experiences, and literacy strategies as pedagogical content tools. Agriculture and science teachers (N=20) participated in two cohorts over two years. We identified six common local agricultural misconception topics: consequences of grain- versus grass-finished beef, hormone-free animal products, genetically modified (GMO) foods, organic food production, animal production environments, and animal agriculture’s role in global warming. Pre-/post- interviews and surveys documented teachers’ incoming misconceptions, as well as their changes in understanding at the institute’s conclusion. title: Measure of Emotional Intelligence in Texas School-Based Agricultural Educators
text_snippet: Measure of Emotional Intelligence in Texas School-Based Agricultural Educators School-Based Agricultural Education programs provide students with academic, leadership, and experiential learning opportunities that require educators to manage complex instructional and relational responsibilities. Framed through human capital theory and emotional intelligence theory, this descriptive, cross-sectional study examined emotional intelligence among school-based agricultural educators in Texas. Data were collected during the 2018–2019 academic year using the Genos Emotional Intelligence Concise Inventory (Self). Usable emotional intelligence responses were analyzed from (N = 495) educators, with demographic differences examined across gender, age, ethnicity, and highest degree attained. Overall emotional intelligence scores exceeded the international benchmark reported for the instrument, with respondents reporting an overall mean score of 119.9 (SD = 14.28). Emotional Reasoning was the highest-scoring sub-category (M = 19.12, SD = 2.85), suggesting strength in using emotional information to guide workplace decisions and communication. title: Contextual Teaching and Learning in Agricultural Education: A Systematic Review
text_snippet: Contextual Teaching and Learning in Agricultural Education: A Systematic Review Limited research has been conducted on contextual teaching and learning (CTL) in agricultural education since it was officially coined in 1998. The founding authors intended CTL to be transdisciplinary and adaptable to different pedagogies. Contextualized teaching is a natural part of education in agriculture, forestry, and natural resource (AFNR) classrooms. A synthesized understanding of CTL’s potential could help teachers improve AFNR education and support academic outcomes. Therefore, the goal of this review was to provide a relevant, unified narrative of CTL’s origin, summarize empirical studies, and identify future directions for CTL in undergraduate agricultural education. We conducted a semi-systematic review of 42 peer-reviewed articles on contextualized teaching and/or learning in AFNR education, using qualitative analysis techniques to describe general characteristics, the operationalization of CTL, research methods, and outcomes. We identified seven unifying themes that organize CTL in AFNR research into five broad areas, which could guide future research. title: Exploring Michigan School-Based Agricultural Educator Retention Since 1917
text_snippet: Exploring Michigan School-Based Agricultural Educator Retention Since 1917 Teacher retention is an ongoing challenge across disciplines, including School-Based Agricultural Education (SBAE). The current study sought to better understand teacher retention via historical quantitative research exploring a database of Michigan SBAE teachers dating back to 1917. Findings indicate the average length of a continuous teaching stretch (i.e., teaching SBAE without leaving the career) was 6.89 years. Teachers who started a continuous teaching stretch between 2000 and 2009 averaged the longest stretch, 10.37 years. Teachers who started a continuous teaching stretch between 2010 and 2019 included the highest proportion who taught for more than five years (i.e., 53.72%). Teacher movement during continuous teaching stretches was also investigated, with results indicating 32.73% of SBAE teachers in Michigan moved schools during a continuous teaching stretch. Teachers who started a continuous teaching stretch between 1930 and 1939 were the most likely to move during a continuous teaching stretch (i.e., 60.36%). title: Validated Route-Aware Method for Longitudinal Analysis of the Journal of the Agricultural Education Archive
text_snippet: Validated Route-Aware Method for Longitudinal Analysis of the Journal of the Agricultural Education Archive A full-corpus longitudinal analysis of the Journal of Agricultural Education (JAE) archive requires validated procedures that can accommodate both optical character recognition (OCR)- dependent historical and born-digital modern manuscripts. This study developed, documented, and validated a route-aware method for full-corpus semantic reconstruction and longitudinal analysis of the JAE archive from 1960 through 2026. The method used separate processing pathways for OCR-dependent legacy manuscripts (1960–1999) and born-digital modern manuscripts (2000–2026). Both pathways converged into targeted section extraction, content-only semantic embedding, and epoch-level metric construction. Validation included a pre-specified OCR audit of the 1985–1994 legacy window, comparison with a 1975–1984 control window, paired correction testing, and a bounded portability assessment using a sampled Journal of Extension corpus. The reconstructed archive included 2,588 articles, of which 2,572 were retained for semantic analysis after excluding non-structured records. title: Returning Teachers as an Underutilized Source of Supply in School-Based Agricultural Education
text_snippet: Returning Teachers as an Underutilized Source of Supply in School-Based Agricultural Education The persistent shortage of school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers necessitates innovative approaches to sustaining the teaching workforce. One underexamined strategy is reengaging returning teachers, defined as licensed SBAE educators who leave the profession and later reenter. This study examined returning teachers as a source of SBAE supply using data from the National Agricultural Education Supply and Demand (NSD) Project. Returning teachers were first identified as a distinct hiring category in 2024. Descriptive analyses were conducted using national and state-level data from 2024 and 2025 to examine trends in gender composition, attrition, hiring sources, regional variation, and the relationship between returning teachers and shortage and shortfall metrics. Results indicate returning teachers comprised approximately 7% of net hires in 2024 and 8% in 2025, although substantial variation existed across states and regions. While returning teachers represented a small share of hires nationally, they accounted for more than 20% of net hires in several states. title: Impact of the Student Teaching Internship on the Emotional Intelligence of Pre-Service School-Based Agricultural Education Teachers
text_snippet: Impact of the Student Teaching Internship on the Emotional Intelligence of Pre-Service School-Based Agricultural Education Teachers This study sought to explore the impact the student teaching internship has on the emotional intelligence of pre-service teachers during the Spring 2025 semester. Objectives for the study were identified as: determine the emotional intelligence level of pre-service teachers prior to their first teaching experience, determine the emotional intelligence level of pre-service teachers just after their first teaching experience, and compare the difference in emotional intelligence scores from before and after the student teaching experience. The population of interest was pre-service school-based agricultural education teachers at Oklahoma State University. The instrument used was the Social-Emotional Competence Teacher Rating Scale (SECTRS) with a retrospective pretest-posttest approach. Teacher-student relationships and interpersonal relationships were found to be the two components of Emotional Intelligence impacted most by the student teaching internship. This study highlights the necessity of incorporating emotional intelligence training into teacher preparation programs to better prepare preservice teachers for the demands of teaching school-based agricultural education.

title: Authentic Research, Real Gains: Evaluation of the University of Florida Research and Extension Experiences for Circularity and Digitalization Skill Development of Undergraduates
text_snippet: Authentic Research, Real Gains: Evaluation of the University of Florida Research and Extension Experiences for Circularity and Digitalization Skill Development of Undergraduates This study examines the University of Florida Circularity and Digitalization Skills Research and Extension Experiences for Undergraduates (Florida’s CD-Skills REEU) to answer: Is the program successful, and what features or mechanisms make it so? We conducted a qualitative outcomes-focused program evaluation with embedded process evaluation elements using semi-structured group interview and a nested codebook (five themes, twenty subcodes) interpreted through a theory-as-lens framework. title: Navigating Extension’s Future: A Synthesis of Contemporary Research for Extension Directors
text_snippet: Navigating Extension’s Future: A Synthesis of Contemporary Research for Extension Directors Cooperative Extension operates within an increasingly complex environment shaped by fiscal pressures, demographic change, evolving public expectations, technological transformation, and workforce challenges. Although research has explored leadership competencies among Extension administrators, fewer studies have examined how Directors understand and respond to contemporary environmental challenges. This integrative review synthesizes findings from a multi-state qualitative study of Extension administrators and subsequent peer-reviewed scholarship derived from that program of research. The purpose of this manuscript is to identify leadership implications emerging from the intersection of administrator experiences and contemporary Extension literature. An integrative review methodology was employed, drawing upon findings from the foundational qualitative study and related scholarship published in the Journal of Agricultural Education, The Journal of Agricultural Education and Extension, Journal of Extension, Journal of Human Sciences and Extension, and Journal of Youth Development. title: Multi-Temporal Perspectives on Teacher Job Satisfaction and Intent to Remain an Agricultural Educator
text_snippet: Multi-Temporal Perspectives on Teacher Job Satisfaction and Intent to Remain an Agricultural Educator The agriculture teacher shortage continues to be the most daunting challenge within the discipline. Within agricultural education scholarship exploring this challenge, job satisfaction and agriculture teachers’ intent to remain in the profession are commonly used constructs. An opportunity existed to diversify the perspectives of these commonly explored constructs by using a multi-temporal approach in which teachers were asked to report their past, present, and future job satisfaction and intent to remain. The current study seized that opportunity through survey research methods in Michigan grounded in the Integrated Model of Work Motivation. Findings from this research suggest minimal differences in how teachers perceived their past, present, and future job satisfaction; alternatively, present intent to remain was consistently higher than past or future intent to remain. This study also illuminates populations of agriculture teachers in Michigan which report lower job satisfaction and intent to remain across temporal perspectives, including suburban agriculture teachers, mid-career teachers, and female agriculture teachers. title: Evaluating Hypothetical Case Scenarios as a Tool to Develop Systems Thinking: A Social Cognitive Theory Analysis
text_snippet: Evaluating Hypothetical Case Scenarios as a Tool to Develop Systems Thinking: A Social Cognitive Theory Analysis The food, agriculture, and natural resource (FANR) domain has numerous complex and interconnected challenges often termed “wicked problems,” which need to be addressed using novel techniques. Systems thinking has been identified as an important competency needed to address complex FANR challenges but implementing systems-oriented developmental approaches is often hindered by a lack of effective tools that can be easily integrated into formal or non-formal programs. One promising strategy is the use of Hypothetical Case Scenarios (HCS), which immerse individuals in realistic situations and encourage them to make decisions reflecting situations one might encounter in real life where no clear, correct options are obvious. While the use of HCS shows potential, limited research has explored its application in a FANR context. This study evaluated the use of HCS as a tool to develop systems thinking among individuals. Guided by social cognitive theory, the study incorporated the Kirkpatrick evaluation model to empirically evaluate the HCS approach. title: Preparing and Supporting Cooperating Teachers for Enhanced Mentorship: Insights from the Student Teaching Experience
text_snippet: Preparing and Supporting Cooperating Teachers for Enhanced Mentorship: Insights from the Student Teaching Experience Nearly half of U.S. teachers leave the profession within their first five years, making teacher retention a persistent concern. High-quality mentorship during the student teaching internship plays a critical role in supporting new teachers, with cooperating teachers serving as key mentors for student teachers. Despite the importance of this relationship, limited research examines the mentoring dynamics between CTs and STs. This mixed-methods study investigates cooperating teacher and student teacher perspectives on mentor–mentee experiences related to 17 identified best practices for mentoring behaviors during student teaching. Findings indicate that student teachers often hold different understandings or needs regarding these best practices than those demonstrated by their cooperating teachers. The identified disparities between cooperating teachers’ perceived mentoring practices and student teachers’ observed experiences suggest a need for further research to better prepare and support cooperating teachers in their essential mentoring roles.

title: Lessons from the Garden: An Autoethnography of Learning and Unlearning in Agricultural Education
text_snippet: Lessons from the Garden: An Autoethnography of Learning and Unlearning in Agricultural Education This autoethnography traces my evolution as a White educator, researcher, and activist working in school and community garden spaces and examines how these experiences cultivated an abolitionist approach to agricultural and civic education. Drawing on frameworks like abolitionist teaching and food justice, I explore how gardens became sites of learning, resistance, and contradiction. Through personal vignettes, field notes, and narrative inquiry, I illustrate how gardening with Black and Brown youth revealed the enduring afterlife of slavery within contemporary food systems and how these insights pushed my practice beyond apolitical garden-based education toward explicit freedom work. I highlight key pedagogical shifts, including recognizing gardens as commons where youth enact mutual aid and democratic decision making; understanding food cultivation as both a civic and abolitionist act; and confronting tensions around my own whiteness, institutional constraints, and the limits of volunteer labor within capitalist systems. title: Developing Teacher Identity Through the Design and Implementation of an Urban Ag+STEM Pathway
text_snippet: Developing Teacher Identity Through the Design and Implementation of an Urban Ag+STEM Pathway This narrative inquiry explores the journey of an urban agriculture teacher and how his experiences informed his professional identity while developing an Ag+STEM career pathway in a STEM-focused urban high school. Drawing on two semi-structured interviews, we tell Dylan’s story– how he cultivated his identity as a School-Based Agricultural Education (SBAE) teacher by focusing on: (1) why he chose to integrate agriculture and STEM, and (2) how he navigated the intersections of his Ag+STEM vision, the challenges he faced, and the instructional strategies he implemented in his classroom. Dylan’s story serves as a microcosm of the experiences of many SBAE teachers striving to establish STEM-focused agricultural programs in urban high schools. His journey offers valuable insights into the development of professional identity as an urban agriculture teacher and the advancement of agriculture and STEM education in urban high schools.

title: “Less About the Sustainability, More About the Economics:” Cotton Growers’ Perceptions of Voluntary Sustainability Programs to Inform Communication Strategy
text_snippet: “Less About the Sustainability, More About the Economics:” Cotton Growers’ Perceptions of Voluntary Sustainability Programs to Inform Communication Strategy This study explored Texas High Plains (THP) cotton producers’ perceptions of sustainable practices, voluntary sustainability programs (VSPs), and the U.S. Cotton Trust Protocol (USCTP), specifically. Using focus groups, the research identified recurring themes in producer opinions on communication strategies, concerns about VSP participation, and motivations for enrollment. The findings highlighted producers’ desire for deeper education about the programs, concerns regarding the program’s trustworthiness, and the need for emphasis on relatable success stories and financial incentives. Applicability to region-specific operations and clear observability of benefits were also determined as critical factors in producers’ decision to adopt sustainable practices. Grounded in the diffusion of innovations theory and social marketing principles, this study highlights the need for tailored communication from VSPs using social marketing to overcome barriers to adoption. title: Saturation of Ease: Why Technical Competence Fails to Drive Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Agricultural Literacy
text_snippet: Saturation of Ease: Why Technical Competence Fails to Drive Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Agricultural Literacy Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces a challenge to agricultural literacy by potentially separating the product of knowledge from the process of synthesis. Participants were a purposive sample of Alabama school-based agricultural education teachers (N = 75). The study examined whether behavioral intention to adopt AI for literacy instruction was associated more strongly with operational competency or perceived pedagogical validity. A regression analysis indicated the model explained 36.2% of the variance in behavioral intention (R² = .362, adjusted R² = .323). The findings revealed a distinction between participants’ high general comfort with technology integration (M = 4.30, SD = .76) and their comparatively lower experiential validation of AI outputs (M = 3.34, SD = .67). title: Using Sense of Community to Inform the Development and Dissemination of Outreach and Extension Programming
text_snippet: Using Sense of Community to Inform the Development and Dissemination of Outreach and Extension Programming Sense of community is a foundational construct for building effective outreach and extension programs, yet few studies examine how sense of community differs across demographic groups that guide audience segmentation. This quantitative study surveyed 3,347 residents of Georgia using the 12-item Brief Sense of Community Scale (composed of four factors: needs fulfillment, group membership, influence, and emotional connection) and six demographic indicators (gender, age, education, employment status, employment level, and metro-urban-rural location). Internal consistency for the overall sense of community index was high (α = .93). One-way ANOVAs showed no gender differences, but significant differences emerged for age, education, employment status, employment level, and metro-urban-rural. Effect sizes were small (ηp2 ≤ .009), indicating nuanced importance of demographic groups. Within the sense of community construct, the needs fulfillment factor had the highest observed mean scores, whereas the influence factor had the lowest observed scores. Results indicate demographic factors such as age, education, and employment status are important for tailoring extension and outreach efforts.

title: Agricultural Science Teachers’ Reported Dispositions of Culturally Relevant Educational Practices: A National Study
text_snippet: Agricultural Science Teachers’ Reported Dispositions of Culturally Relevant Educational Practices: A National Study This study explored the dispositions of school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers toward culturally relevant educational practices. As agricultural education classrooms continue to become more diverse, teachers need effective teaching practices to address the needs of all students. Using nationally distributed electronic survey, responses from 514 agricultural science teachers were analyzed to assess their attitudes across three key subscales: praxis, community, and social justice. The findings indicate that participants strongly valued items related to praxis and community but demonstrated less agreement with statements about social justice. Regression analysis revealed that teachers in suburban and urban settings were more likely to value collaboration and engagement with students, families, and colleagues. These results suggest that while SBAE teachers generally support culturally relevant pedagogy, there are gaps in critical consciousness that may impact implementation.

title: Exploring Usage Patterns of News and Information Sources among Ohio Residents
text_snippet: Exploring Usage Patterns of News and Information Sources among Ohio Residents To navigate everyday issues such as food safety, climate change, water quality, and sustainable practices, credible, accessible, and timely information is essential. Our study assessed how Ohio residents use different news and information sources through the lens of media system dependency theory. We also examined how age, gender, income, community type, and education influence dependency on three types of information sources: traditional media (television, radio, newspapers), new media (websites, social media), and interpersonal sources (family and friends, Extension agents). Using a quantitative survey, data were collected from 515 Ohio residents and analyzed using descriptive statistics and linear regression methods. Results revealed that traditional media were the most frequently used source, whereas interpersonal sources were used the least. Regression results showed that dependency on different media sources is influenced by age and gender. Younger participants relied more on new media, particularly social media, whereas older participants mostly used traditional media. title: Defining Programmatic Balance in School-Based Agricultural Education: A Modified Delphi Study
text_snippet: Defining Programmatic Balance in School-Based Agricultural Education: A Modified Delphi Study The persistent shortage of school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers has generated substantial research on workload, role strain, and work–life balance; however, limited attention has been given to how balance is conceptualized within SBAE programs themselves. Although professional models consistently depict classroom instruction, Supervised Agricultural Experiences (SAE), and FFA as equally important components, the construct of programmatic balance remains largely undefined in the scholarly literature. The purpose of this study was to define programmatic balance by articulating the construct in secondary SBAE through expert consensus. A three-round modified Delphi method was employed with a national panel of SBAE experts representing supervisory and leadership roles in agricultural education across the United States. The panel identified classroom instruction as the foundational element from which SAE and FFA activities are derived and supported. Programmatic balance was further characterized as contextually responsive, student-centered, and community-based, while rejecting rigid or prescriptive models. title: Leadership Journeys of 12 Women in the Wine Industry
text_snippet: Leadership Journeys of 12 Women in the Wine Industry This study discusses the narratives of 12 women who have ascended to leadership roles within the wine industry, shedding light on their diverse experiences, influences, and pathways to leadership. Six key themes emerged from their journeys: diversity of backgrounds, gender barriers, mentorship, community support, getting it done, and a commitment to continuous learning. Despite the majority lacking exposure to the wine industry prior to their careers, these women showcased an ethos of learning and adaptability, drawing from diverse personal and educational backgrounds. Gender biases, though prevalent, were overcome through resilience and transformative leadership, challenging industry stereotypes. The intersectionality of gender roles and motherhood further highlighted some of these women's societal struggles, emphasizing the need for transformative shifts in societal norms. Mentorship emerged as a cornerstone of their professional journeys. Community support, collaborative efforts, and a shared commitment to staying informed were integral to their success and well-being. title: Exploring Agricultural Faculty Perspectives on Culturally Responsive Pedagogy at 1862 and 1890 Land Grant Universities
text_snippet: Exploring Agricultural Faculty Perspectives on Culturally Responsive Pedagogy at 1862 and 1890 Land Grant Universities Historically, the Land Grant University (LGU) system has struggled to engage and support Black agricultural students due to discriminatory practices and inequitable resource allocation between 1862 and 1890 institutions. Despite the success of 1890 LGUs in graduating Black students, limited research explores the specific teaching styles agricultural faculty use to support this demographic. This qualitative study explored how faculty at 1862 and 1890 LGUs define and implement Culturally Responsive Pedagogy (CRP). Using semi-structured interviews with 11 faculty members and reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined faculty motivations and the institutional affordances or constraints they face to implement CRP. Findings indicate that faculty define CRP through cultural competence and student-centeredness, emphasizing trust-building and leveraging students’ lived experiences to combat traditional Westernized instruction. Most participants described a "switch moment"—a specific event or realization regarding social inequities—that motivated their transition to CRP practitioners. title: Predicting High School Students’ Situated Expectancy-Value Motivation Regarding Food System STEM Projects
text_snippet: Predicting High School Students’ Situated Expectancy-Value Motivation Regarding Food System STEM Projects The study predicted high school students’ self-efficacy (as confirmed by Exploratory Factor Analysis, EFA) based on Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) variables. A convenience sample of 160 students from four Indiana high schools who had participated in food system science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) projects was used. Quantitative data were collected through the Food System Motivation Questionnaire to measure two self-efficacy variables and five SEVT variables. The data obtained were analyzed using Principal Components Analysis, descriptive statistics, simple linear correlations, and multiple regression. Qualitative data were collected via focus group interviews and analyzed through thematic (deductive) and pattern coding. Triangulation was used to analyze both data types. The findings showed that students’ motivation to solve complex food system problems through integrated STEM learning was reflected in their learning experiences and helped teachers make relevant connections. title: Using Virtual Reality Trainers to Increase Welding Self-Efficacy in Preservice School-Based Agricultural Education Teachers: An Exploratory Case Study
text_snippet: Using Virtual Reality Trainers to Increase Welding Self-Efficacy in Preservice School-Based Agricultural Education Teachers: An Exploratory Case Study Many school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers teach agricultural mechanics, giving them a critical role in training the in-demand welders of tomorrow. However, limited postsecondary coursework in agricultural mechanics can leave preservice SBAE teachers underprepared to teach in a laboratory setting. Virtual Reality (VR) technology has been used in welding and other disciplines to supplement instruction when training in a live setting is dangerous or costly. While prior research has linked VR welding technology to improved skill development and self-efficacy among agriculture majors and members of the workforce, no such study has been done with preservice SBAE teachers. The purpose of this exploratory case study was to examine changes in welding self-efficacy among preservice teachers at Tarleton State University. Eight students participated in a pre-treatment self-efficacy survey, a two-hour practice session with a VR welding trainer, a two-hour live welding training session, and a post-treatment self-efficacy survey. title: Framing Agriculture from Past to Present: A Historical Analysis of FFA Magazine Covers from 1952 to 2024
text_snippet: Framing Agriculture from Past to Present: A Historical Analysis of FFA Magazine Covers from 1952 to 2024 Despite some considering print media to be nearing an end, researchers have continued to find the importance and impact that print media still has on its audience and in the broader media landscape. Specifically, the New Horizons magazine, analyzed in this study, reaches nearly one million people and showcases the FFA and the agricultural industry, supported by the National FFA Organization. Utilizing framing theory and visual rhetoric, a historical analysis of the covers was conducted to identify trends in the portrayal of agriculture throughout the decades. In the analysis, 392 covers were collected and coded, both broadly and by sub-categories, using the National FFA Proficiency categories and two additional categories of FFA-Related and Other. Findings from the analysis showed that the Careers category had the most associated covers (n = 106), whereas the Crops category was represented the least (n = 52). Moreover, the Careers and Animals categories were frequently identified until the 1990s, when FFA-Related, including sub-categories such as Official Dress and Alumni, became more represented. title: Attitudes Toward Biotechnology: Snapshot of Professional Development, Barriers, and Motivation in Agricultural Education
text_snippet: Attitudes Toward Biotechnology: Snapshot of Professional Development, Barriers, and Motivation in Agricultural Education With the anticipated surge in the global population over the next 25 years and beyond, there is a significant need for agriculturalists to produce more using less. Biotechnology is one way we can ensure that the ever-growing population will continue to be sustained in satisfying global food, fiber, and fuel demands. However, in order to enter careers in this career area, and be aware of these innovative technologies so that consumers of today and tomorrow can make informed decisions, education about biotechnology is essential. The purpose of this study was to review teachers’ confidence level in teaching biotechnology concepts, professional development activities, motivation to teach the concepts, and perception of available resources. The study was conducted utilizing a quantitative instrument administered to a group of 74 agricultural educators representing 19 states, who indicated interest in teaching biotechnology, or participation in biotechnology professional development experiences. title: Call to Better Qual: The Science and Art of Qualitative Research Interviewing
text_snippet: Call to Better Qual: The Science and Art of Qualitative Research Interviewing Substantial efforts across the qualitative landscape of the Journal of Agricultural Education occur through interviewing. Yet little exists in our discipline to support rigorous use of this methodological tool. This practical manuscript uses philosophy, methodology, theory, our own experience, and wisdom from wide-ranging sources to provide a guide to both the art and science of interviewing for novice and advanced researchers alike. In exploring the science of interviewing, we outline question types, interpretive frameworks, interview structures, and methodological assumptions. In advancing the art of interviewing, we align with the CHE framework focusing on the connectivity, humanness, and empathy required to engage in research with our participants rather than on or about them. Finally, we conclude with a call for reflexivity as a unifying means of conducting rigorous, well-articulated, and deeply meaningful interviews as we continually strive to improve as research instruments.

title: Understanding Healthy Eating Behaviors Using Theory of Planned Behavior and Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change
text_snippet: Understanding Healthy Eating Behaviors Using Theory of Planned Behavior and Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change Our study assesses participants' engagement in healthy eating behaviors and examines the factors that predict it. The Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and the Transtheoretical Model (TTM) were integrated to develop a conceptual model for exploring key research questions. Participants (n = 1,528) were recruited using quota-based nonprobability sampling, and data were collected through an online cross-sectional survey. The effects of TPB variables (attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control [PBC]) on participants at different stages of behavior change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance) were assessed using descriptive statistics. Respondents were categorized into two groups: intention (cognitive phase: precontemplation, contemplation, and preparation) and behavior (actual behavior: action and maintenance). The effects of TPB variables on these two groups were assessed using binary logistic regression. Participants held mixed attitudes toward healthy eating, injunctive norms, and PBC. title: Navigating a Multiracial Identity in Agricultural Education: The Impact of Racial Imposter Phenomenon
text_snippet: Navigating a Multiracial Identity in Agricultural Education: The Impact of Racial Imposter Phenomenon The racial demographic of the United States is changing, and the increase in multiracial children is substantial. This study explores the experiences of multiracial graduates from secondary agricultural education programs, focusing on the presence of the racial impostor phenomenon (Racial IP) related to their multiracial identities. With nearly half of the multiracial population in the U.S. under 18, understanding the racial dynamics faced by multiracial youth is essential, particularly in educational contexts where monoracial norms often prevail. This multiple-case, qualitative study involved in-depth interviews with eight multiracial individuals, all graduates of secondary agricultural education. The study's theoretical framework leverages Clance’s and Imes’s (1978) impostor phenomenon, adapted to explore how racial impostorism influences multiracial individuals’ identities in predominantly White educational settings. Findings indicated that all participants exhibited at least two dimensions of IP, with four dimensions frequently observed: Need to Be Special / The Very Best, Superwoman/Superman Aspects, Fear of Failure, and Denial of Competence and Denial of Praise. title: Evaluating Retention Factors of Teachers Implementing CASE Curriculum in Agricultural Education Programs
text_snippet: Evaluating Retention Factors of Teachers Implementing CASE Curriculum in Agricultural Education Programs Across the United States, there continues to be a significant shortage of agricultural educators. As a result, retaining quality and qualified agricultural educators is an urgent need. The Curriculum for Agricultural Science Education (CASE) provides agricultural educators the opportunity to earn curriculum certification in a range of agriculturally focused content areas. Teachers can receive training and access to teaching materials and resources to implement the CASE curriculum within their agricultural education programs, providing students with rich, inquiry-based learning experiences. The purpose of this study was to determine if there is a connection between SBAE teachers’ earning of at least one CASE certification and their reports of satisfying a multitude of retention factors within the school-based agricultural education (SBAE) profession. As such, this study examined perceptions associated with CASE implementation, which connect to retention factors, as opposed to causal effects on retention in and of itself. title: African-American Community-based Programs Leaders’ Motivations and Educational Space Serving African American Youth : African-American Agricultural Centered Community-based Organization Leaders' Motivations
text_snippet: African-American Community-based Programs Leaders’ Motivations and Educational Space Serving African American Youth : African-American Agricultural Centered Community-based Organization Leaders' Motivations African-Americans have historically faced limited access to agricultural education due to systemic barriers and the negative perception of agriculture, often associated with slavery, exploitation, and land dispossession. Despite these challenges, African-American-led community-based organizations have emerged as alternative learning spaces for agricultural education. This study examines African-American leaders and their motivations for establishing and directing agricultural and STEM-focused community-based programs. Using purposive sampling, eight program leaders were selected, and semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore their reasons for engaging Black youth in agricultural education and the ways these programs function as sites of social and cultural capital formation. Findings indicate that program leaders cultivate social capital by fostering mentorship, intergenerational knowledge transfer, and community networks. At the same time, they strengthen cultural capital by embedding Black history, African agricultural traditions, and experiential learning into agricultural education. title: Professional Development Preferences of Oklahoma Agricultural Educators
text_snippet: Professional Development Preferences of Oklahoma Agricultural Educators In part of a larger mission to address professional development among SBAE teachers, this study is specifically targeting the preferences of SBAE teachers in Oklahoma. A non-experimental survey research study employed a census approach for SBAE teachers in Oklahoma. This study implemented crosstabs analysis in SPSS to compare personal and professional characteristics and professional development preferences. The majority of participants prefer to receive professional development in-person at Oklahoma State University, based on this study. Although professional development may adapt over time, participants indicated an interest in participating, therefore taking personal responsibility for professional growth. Regardless of the physical location of professional development, perhaps a need exists to share responsibility for in-service education programs across stakeholder groups in a single location.

title: Familismo in Action: Community, Culture, and Leadership Development through a Student-Led Event
text_snippet: Familismo in Action: Community, Culture, and Leadership Development through a Student-Led Event Undergraduate leadership development is an increasingly important component of agricultural education as institutions prepare graduates to address complex 21st-century challenges. Student-led activities provide experiential learning opportunities that cultivate leadership, community engagement, and career readiness. This qualitative study explored the leadership experiences of undergraduates who organized the 26 Hours of Science and Technology (26 Hours) conference, a culturally grounded event hosted by the Latinos in Agriculture Club (LIA) at California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) Guided by Kolb’s (1984) experiential learning model and the holistic framework, the study examined how students engaged in concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Data were collected through two triadic focus group interviews (n = 6) with student leaders serving as co-hosts, committee heads, volunteers, and event support. Thematic analysis revealed four themes aligned with Kolb’s cycle: variation in leadership roles (experience), student fulfillment (reflection), student growth (conceptualization), and impact expansion (application)

title: Towards the Integration of Generative AI into the Cooperative Extension Service: Insights for Guiding Professional Development
text_snippet: Towards the Integration of Generative AI into the Cooperative Extension Service: Insights for Guiding Professional Development Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) can enhance the efficiency, productivity and accessibility of Cooperative Extension Service’ (CES) work, yet empirically grounded guidance for its ethical and effective utilization remains limited. Guided by the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, this study employed a three-round electronic Delphi technique involving six CES professionals experienced in Gen AI applications, to build consensus on CES-appropriate Gen AI tools, compatible Extension tasks, training and resource needs, barriers to utilization, and best practices. Within the technological context, Copilot, ChatGPT, and Gemini (Advanced) were identified as the most suitable Gen AI tools for Extension work. These tools were perceived as most effective in supporting audio-to-text and text-to-audio conversion, administrative writing tasks, and idea generation for research, Extension programming, and answering clientele questions. The organizational context revealed key barriers: limited ability to blend professional expertise with AI-generated content, low Gen AI/digital literacy, and concerns about overreliance on AI undermining critical thinking. title: Stability of Needs Identified using the Borich Model and Ranked Discrepancy Model: Influence of Sample Size and Data Distribution
text_snippet: Stability of Needs Identified using the Borich Model and Ranked Discrepancy Model: Influence of Sample Size and Data Distribution The Borich model has been widely used for the past 40 years to assess professional development needs. The more recent creation of the Ranked Discrepancy Model (RDM) introduced another option for researchers and therefore the need to investigate the appropriateness of the approaches for different research scenarios. In this study, we have sought to answer questions of how sample size and different data distributions affect the stability of results. Using a pre-existing dataset, we analyzed the data using the Borich model and RDM with samples of 25, 50, 75, 100, and 150, and compared the results between a semi-normal distribution and a heavily skewed distribution (simulated from the real data set). We found that the Borich model was more stable compared to the RDM when there was a small data set that was semi-normally distributed. The RDM was more stable with heavily skewed data, regardless of sample size. Both models showed greater stability with larger sample sizes. title: Inclusion for All? Opportunities and Challenges of Including Students with Diverse Needs in FFA Activities
text_snippet: Inclusion for All? Opportunities and Challenges of Including Students with Diverse Needs in FFA Activities The purpose of this study is to examine the experiences of North Carolina high school agriculture teachers with incorporating students with diverse needs in FFA. More specifically, this study seeks to identify and describe the challenges and suggested improvements for incorporating students with diverse needs in FFA, determine inclusionary practices teachers utilize to encourage students with diverse needs’ FFA participation that teachers perceive as successful, and identify the motivations of teachers incorporating students with diverse needs in FFA. The three-circle model of agricultural education served as a conceptual framework to this study. This qualitative study used the interviews of eight North Carolina high school agriculture teachers as the primary method of data collection. Through these interviews the following themes emerged: the value of relationship building and the challenges with competition. It is recommended by the researcher that pre-service and in-service training be implemented related to the inclusion of students with diverse needs in FFA. title: Determining the Antecedents of Preparation of SBAE Teachers Who Effectively Facilitate Learning in SBAE Laboratories
text_snippet: Determining the Antecedents of Preparation of SBAE Teachers Who Effectively Facilitate Learning in SBAE Laboratories The purpose of this qualitative study was to discover how expert school-based agricultural education (SBAE) teachers describe the experiences which best prepared them to have the ability to teach, manage, and facilitate learning activities in agricultural education laboratories. SBAE teachers teach technical skills and how to safely and properly use equipment associated with those skills, such as electrical, welding, woodworking, greenhouse watering and heating systems, aquaculture systems, and agricultural mechanics. All of these skills are demonstrated, practiced, and are mastered in agricultural education laboratories. Perhaps adequate training of pre-service SBAE teachers, particularly in the most common laboratories such as greenhouses, agricultural mechanics labs, carpentry labs, and welding laboratories would help mitigate the growing SBAE teacher attrition rate and ensure that proper laboratory teaching techniques and management is implemented. title: Cultivating Wellness: An Explanatory Mixed Methods Study of Ohio School-Based Agricultural Education Teacher’s Personal Wellness
text_snippet: Cultivating Wellness: An Explanatory Mixed Methods Study of Ohio School-Based Agricultural Education Teacher’s Personal Wellness Wellness as a concept can be characterized by holistic, multidimensional, and integrate elements and has been applied and practiced in varied ways depending on culture. The Indivisible Self, a model refined by science, guides this study which aimed to apply a holistic view of wellness to a sample of Ohio SBAE teachers. The study seeks to understand how SBAE teachers conceptualize and manifest wellness in their lives, examining both wellness measures and teacher experiences. The research incorporated quantitative and qualitative methodologies specifically employing an explanatory mixed-method sequential design. Quantitative methods utilized the 5-Factor Wellness Evaluation of Lifestyle (5F-Wel) with 212 completed responses from Ohio SBAE teachers to identify participants for the qualitative phase. Interviews were completed with nine teachers. Quantitative results indicated the sample exhibits more healthful behaviors than unhealthful ones, with social wellness as a notable strength.
